heading: Selected Engineering Challenges
subtitle: Case studies drawn from consulting work across regulated, security-sensitive and enterprise domains.

studies.title: Centralized Transaction & Certification Platform
studies.summaryQuote: Designing transaction flows where correctness matters more than convenience.
studies.contextNote: Simplified architecture based on patterns used in enterprise financial and certification systems (drawn from work on a centralized application for ANCERT, Spain). Details intentionally generalized to protect client confidentiality.
studies.problem: A national certification authority needed to consolidate a range of manual, paper-driven and fragmented internal processes into a single centralized application, without disrupting operations for the teams already depending on the existing tooling.

responsibilities: Authenticates and authorizes the caller
Validates request shape before it reaches business logic
Applies rate limiting
Coordinates the transaction lifecycle
Enforces business rules
Maintains state transitions
Handles retries and failures
Checks business rules before any state changes
Rejects malformed or fraudulent requests
Maintains the authoritative balance and transaction history
Enforces double-entry accounting invariants
Deduplicates retried requests using an idempotency key
Returns the original result instead of reprocessing
Persists transaction state within ACID boundaries
Isolates concurrent writes to the same account
Publishes a durable record of what happened
Decouples the transaction path from downstream consumers
Builds a tamper-evident trail for compliance and dispute resolution
Informs the client and internal teams of the outcome
Reconciles with the external payment provider

decisions.question: Why a centralized transaction service instead of letting each module write to the database directly?
decisions.answer: Funneling every state change through one orchestrator made it possible to enforce consistency rules and auditing in a single place instead of duplicating (and eventually diverging) that logic across modules.

decisions.question: Why idempotency as its own concern instead of relying on clients not to retry?
decisions.answer: Retries are guaranteed to happen at scale — network timeouts, double-clicks, mobile connectivity drops. An idempotency key per request meant a retried transaction replayed the original result instead of creating a duplicate.

decisions.question: Why an event stream alongside the synchronous path to the database?
decisions.answer: The transaction itself needed a synchronous, consistent write. But audit, notification and settlement only needed eventual consistency — decoupling them through events kept the critical path short and let each consumer fail independently.

decisions.question: What happens when an external settlement provider fails?
decisions.answer: The transaction is already durably committed before settlement is attempted, so a provider failure triggers a retry with backoff, then a timeout into a compensating flow and reconciliation — it never leaves the ledger in an ambiguous state.

studies.title: Document Signing Workflow
studies.summaryQuote: Long-running workflows where every step needs to be provably correct.
studies.contextNote: Drawn from work in the certification and digital-signature domain (ANCERT, Spain) — details generalized to protect client confidentiality.
studies.problem: Documents needed to move through identity verification, signature collection and legal auditability without losing state if a user dropped off mid-flow, and without giving up cryptographic guarantees for the sake of convenience.

responsibilities: Confirms the signer is who they claim to be before any signature is collected
Re-verifies the signer at the moment of signing, not just at session start
Applies a cryptographic signature bound to the exact document content
Runs under an idempotency key so a retried request can't produce a second signature
Appends every step as an immutable, timestamped record
Reconstructs the full history for legal disputes

decisions.question: Why make every step idempotent instead of relying on the client to avoid duplicate requests?
decisions.answer: Network retries and user double-clicks are guaranteed to happen at scale. Idempotency keys per step meant a retried request just replayed the same result instead of creating a second, conflicting signature.

decisions.question: Why keep the audit trail as an append-only log instead of updating a status field?
decisions.answer: Legal auditability requires reconstructing exactly what happened and when, not just the current state — an append-only trail preserves that history even if a later step corrects an earlier one.

studies.title: Identity & Wallet Authentication
studies.summaryQuote: Letting users authenticate with a wallet without reinventing identity management.
studies.contextNote: A representative architecture drawn from identity and authentication work across consulting engagements, generalized to protect client confidentiality.
studies.problem: An application needed to support wallet-based authentication alongside conventional login, without building a custom identity provider from scratch or compromising on standard protocols.

responsibilities: Issues and validates OAuth2 / OIDC tokens
Delegates wallet signature verification to a custom authentication flow
Manages session and token lifecycle for every downstream service
Trusts a single token format regardless of how the user logged in
Never handles raw credentials or private keys
Signs a challenge to prove ownership of the private key
Returns the signature for Keycloak to verify

decisions.question: Why Keycloak instead of a hand-rolled identity provider?
decisions.answer: Identity is a solved problem with sharp edges (token lifecycle, revocation, standards compliance). Keycloak let the team extend a battle-tested OIDC provider with a custom wallet authentication flow instead of owning all of that surface area.

decisions.question: Why treat wallet auth as another Keycloak authentication flow instead of a parallel system?
decisions.answer: Keeping wallet login inside the same identity provider meant every downstream service still trusted one token format and one session model, regardless of how the user proved who they were.
